blocks.text: The Moderation API is OpenAI's dedicated endpoint for classifying a piece of text, or an image, against a fixed set of policy categories such as hate, harassment, self-harm, sexual content, and violence, giving a concrete, ready-made implementation of the output filtering and input validation concepts covered generically in the earlier Prompt Security module.

This topic covers the request shape, the category flags and confidence scores returned, moderating both text and images, using moderation as a pre-filter on user input and a post-filter on model output, its cost, and its real limitations.
1. What the Moderation API Is

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A piece of text or model output sent to the moderation endpoint comes back with category flags and confidence scores

blocks.text: Where the earlier Prompt Security module covered the general ideas of input validation and output filtering, the Moderation API is one specific, concrete tool for actually doing that filtering, a separate endpoint you call alongside Chat Completions, not something bundled automatically into every request.
2. The Request Shape

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A moderation request carries the text or image to be classified

blocks.text: A moderation request accepts either a single string or an array of strings, applying the same JSON request body mechanics covered in the API Request and Response module, and returns one result object per input.

code.content:
response = client.moderations.create(
    model="omni-moderation-latest",
    input="I want to hurt someone who wronged me.",
)
result = response.results[0]
print(result.flagged)

blocks.text: 3. Category Flags

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Each moderation result carries a boolean flag for several fixed policy categories

blocks.text: Every result carries a boolean for each of a fixed set of categories: hate, harassment, self_harm, sexual, and violence, along with several more specific subcategories. Any one category being true is enough to mark the overall result as flagged.
4. Category Scores

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Beyond the boolean flags, each result also carries a confidence score per category

blocks.text: Alongside the boolean categories field, a result also carries category_scores, one confidence value per category between zero and one. A caller with stricter requirements than the default boolean threshold can apply its own, tighter cutoff directly against these scores.
5. Moderating Images Too

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: The newer omni-moderation model accepts image input using the same category flag structure as text

blocks.text: The newer omni-moderation model accepts image input as well as text, applying to a user-uploaded image the same category flags and scores used for text, useful for platforms that let users upload images alongside text, exactly the kind of input the Vision API topic covers a model actually reasoning about.
6. Moderation as a Pre-Filter on Input

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Flagged user input is rejected before ever reaching the model, unflagged input is forwarded normally

blocks.text: Running every incoming user message through moderation before it ever reaches Chat Completions catches clearly policy-violating input early, before spending a model call on it at all, and before that input can influence a response through prompt injection, covered in the earlier Prompt Security module.
7. Moderation as a Post-Filter on Output

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Flagged model output is held back from the end user, unflagged output is displayed normally

blocks.text: Running a model's own generated response back through moderation before displaying it catches the rarer case where a model itself produces something policy-violating, a genuine, concrete implementation of the output filtering concept from the earlier module, distinct from filtering the user's own input.
8. Cost

Unlike essentially every other endpoint covered in this module, the Moderation API is free to use, removing cost as any reason at all not to run it on both sides of every interaction, incoming user input and outgoing model output alike.
9. Limitations

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Moderation is one useful signal among several, not a complete defense by itself

blocks.text: Moderation is trained against a fixed set of categories and will not catch every possible harm, and a determined adversary using the jailbreak techniques covered in the earlier module can sometimes phrase content to slip past it. It belongs alongside sanitization, guardrails, and the red-teaming discipline covered earlier, not as a replacement for any of them.

blocks.title: Layered Defense, Not a Silver Bullet
blocks.content: Treat a passing moderation result as one signal among several, not proof that a piece of content is genuinely safe on its own.

blocks.text: Worked Example

A community platform runs every user-submitted comment through the Moderation API before it is ever shown to other users or passed along to a model for a generated reply. A comment whose flagged field comes back true is automatically held for manual review instead of being published immediately, while everything else is published right away.

The same platform also moderates every model-generated reply before displaying it, catching the rare case where a generated response itself drifts into flagged territory, exactly the post-filter pattern covered earlier, giving the platform coverage on both the incoming and outgoing side of the conversation.
Common Mistakes

items: Treating a passing moderation result as a complete guarantee of safety rather than one useful signal among several
Checking only the overall flagged boolean and ignoring the more specific per-category scores entirely
Moderating only user input and never checking the model's own generated output
Assuming moderation happens automatically inside Chat Completions rather than being its own separate endpoint to call

blocks.text: Practice

Send three different pieces of text to the Moderation API: one clearly benign, one clearly policy-violating, and one borderline. Print the flagged boolean and the category_scores for all three, and identify which specific category drove the borderline case's score.
Key Takeaway

The Moderation API is a free, dedicated endpoint returning both boolean category flags and confidence scores for text and image input alike, giving a concrete implementation of the input validation and output filtering ideas from the Prompt Security module, best used as one layer alongside sanitization and guardrails on both the input and output side of every interaction, not as a standalone guarantee of safety.
